title: Word Frequency
statement:
On LeetCode this is a Bash problem: write a command that reports how many times each word occurs in the text file `words.txt`. The app has no shell, so here you write a JavaScript function `wordFrequency(content)`. It receives the whole text of the file and returns exactly what the command would output, with lines joined by `\n` and no final line break.

- The text holds only lowercase letters, spaces and line breaks (`\n`). A word is a run of lowercase letters; words are separated by one or more spaces or line breaks, and the text may also start or end with them.
- Output one line per distinct word in the form `word count`: the word, a single space, then the number of times it occurs.
- Order the lines from the most frequent word to the least frequent. No two distinct words occur the same number of times, so this order is unique.
- If the file contains no words, return the empty string.
constraints: content contains only lowercase English letters, spaces and \n
No two distinct words have the same count

notes:
## Intuition

Counting is a job for a map from word to count; the only extra work is cutting the text into words and ordering the result by count. The shell does the same with a pipe:

```bash
tr -s ' ' '\n' < words.txt | grep -v '^$' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | awk '{ print $2, $1 }'
```

- `tr -s ' ' '\n'` turns every space into a line break and squeezes runs of line breaks into one, so each word sits on its own line.
- `grep -v '^$'` drops the empty line left by leading spaces or a leading line break.
- `sort` puts equal words next to each other, because `uniq` only merges neighbours.
- `uniq -c` collapses each group into one line with its count in front: `4 the`.
- `sort -rn` orders those lines by the count, as numbers, largest first.
- `awk '{ print $2, $1 }'` swaps the two fields to get `the 4`.

An awk-only version counts in an array: `awk '{ for (i = 1; i <= NF; i++) c[$i]++ } END { for (w in c) print w, c[w] }' words.txt | sort -k2,2nr`.

## Approach

1. Split `content` on runs of whitespace into `words`.
2. Skip the empty strings the split leaves when the text starts or ends with whitespace; add 1 to `counts` for every other word.
3. Turn `counts` into `[word, count]` pairs in `entries` and sort them by count, largest first.
4. Format each pair as `word count` and join the `lines` with `\n`.

## Example 1, step by step

`content` is `"the day is sunny the the\nthe sunny is is\n"`.

- The split gives `the, day, is, sunny, the, the, the, sunny, is, is` and one trailing `''`, which is skipped.
- `counts` ends as `the → 4, day → 1, is → 3, sunny → 2`.
- Sorting by count gives `the 4, is 3, sunny 2, day 1`.
- Joined: `"the 4\nis 3\nsunny 2\nday 1"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + k log k) for n characters and k distinct words: one pass to count, then a sort of the k pairs.
- Space: O(n) for the split words and the map.

## Pitfalls

- `split(' ')` keeps empty strings between double spaces and ignores line breaks; split on `/\s+/` and skip `''`.
- Sorting counts as text puts `9` above `10`: compare numbers (`b[1] - a[1]`), and use `sort -n` in the shell.
- `uniq -c` without a `sort` before it counts only runs of neighbours, so a word that appears twice apart is listed twice.
- A file of only spaces has no words: the answer is `''`, not a line for the empty word.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `content` | the whole text of `words.txt` |
| `counts` | map from each word to the number of times it occurs |
| `words` | the pieces of `content` between whitespace runs |
| `entries` | the `[word, count]` pairs, sorted by count |
| `lines` | the formatted output lines `word count` |

narration.1: wordFrequency receives the whole file as one string and returns what the pipe would print.
narration.2: counts maps each word to how many times it has appeared so far.
narration.3: Cut the text at every run of spaces and line breaks; leading or trailing whitespace leaves an empty piece.
narration.5: An empty piece is not a word, so it is skipped.
narration.8: Add one to this word, starting from 0 the first time it is seen.
narration.10: Turn the map into [word, count] pairs so they can be sorted.
narration.11: Sort by count as numbers, largest first; counts are unique, so the order is fixed.
narration.12: Format each pair as the word, a space and its count.
narration.13: Join the lines with line breaks, without one at the end.
